summary: Specifies a packetization scheme for carrying uncompressed video in RTP. It supports a range of standard- and high-definition formats, including television formats such as ITU BT.601 and SMPTE standards. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines how to carry uncompressed video in RTP packets. Each packet identifies the scan-line data it contains so a receiver can place the samples back into the video frame.

subtitle: A packet format for sending uncompressed video over RTP, one scan line or line fragment at a time.

tldr.problem: Uncompressed video formats need a common way to travel in RTP despite differences in image dimensions, color sampling, and sample depth.
tldr.mechanism: The format sends active video samples in scan-line units. Payload headers identify each line, its pixel offset, its length, and an extended sequence number.
tldr.outcome: One payload scheme covers several RGB and YCbCr formats, but the RFC warns that the required bandwidth can be very high. RFC 4175 is updated by RFC 4421.

today: RFC 4175 is a Proposed Standard, published in September 2005, and is updated by RFC 4421. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: A Shared Format for Uncompressed Video
sections.content:
RFC 4175 defines an RTP payload format for uncompressed, studio-quality video. It covers formats including ITU-R BT.601, SMPTE 274M, and SMPTE 296M, whose details differ but whose structure is similar.

The format is designed to extend to other similar video formats. It carries active samples rather than horizontal and vertical blanking, and relies on session signaling to describe the sample format.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives RTP a common packet format for uncompressed video. A session description tells the receiver how to interpret the samples.

sections.title: Packetizing Scan Lines
sections.content:
The sender divides each scan line into one or more RTP packets. A packet may also contain more than one line. If a complete line exceeds the network MTU, it SHOULD be split into packets smaller than that MTU. Only active samples are included; inactive samples and blanking intervals SHOULD NOT be sent.

Color sampling can cause neighboring pixels to share samples. The format therefore groups pixels into a pixel group, or pgroup, that occupies a whole number of octets and keeps shared samples together. A sender MUST NOT split a pgroup between packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Packets carry active video data in scan-line order. Pixels that share color samples stay together in complete groups, so the receiver can decode them correctly.

sections.title: RTP and Line Headers
sections.content:
After the standard RTP header, a packet has a 2-octet extension to the sequence number and a 6-octet header for each line or partial line. The extension combines with RTP's sequence number to form a 32-bit value. Each line header contains its data length, field identifier, line number, continuation bit, and pixel offset.

The data length MUST be a multiple of the pgroup size. The marker bit identifies the last packet of a progressive frame or an interlaced field. Packets from different frames or fields MUST NOT be mixed, and packets belonging to one frame or field share its timestamp.
sections.plainLanguage: Each line header tells the receiver which line is present and where its first pixel belongs. The extended sequence number helps distinguish packet order at high data rates.

sections.title: Packing Color Samples
sections.content:
Samples may use 8-, 10-, 12-, or 16-bit values. The order and pgroup size depend on the sampling format, including RGB, RGBA, BGR, BGRA, and several YCbCr sampling modes. For example, YCbCr 4:2:2 groups two adjacent pixels so their shared chrominance samples remain together.

When a scan line ends partway through a pgroup, the sender MUST fill the remaining bits with zero and the receiver MUST ignore that fill. Progressive 4:2:0 video sends samples from two consecutive lines together and identifies the first line in the pair.
sections.plainLanguage: Color formats pack samples differently, and the pgroup rules keep shared samples together. Any unused bits at the end of a line are zero-filled and ignored by the receiver.

sections.title: Video Parameters and Session Description
sections.content:
The registered media type is video/raw. Required parameters describe the RTP clock rate, sampling method, width, height, sample depth, and colorimetry. Width and height each range from 1 to 32767. Optional parameters can describe interlacing, field order, chroma position, and gamma.

When SDP describes the RTP session, the media type appears in the m= line, the payload format appears in a=rtpmap, and the remaining parameters appear in a=fmtp. The receiver learns the sample format out of band rather than from the packet data.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending video, the session description states the image size and sample format. The RTP packets then carry data using that agreed description.

sections.title: Security and Bandwidth
sections.content:
The security considerations of RTP and the RTP profile apply. Confidentiality requires encryption. The RFC says receiver processing cost is not significantly uneven, but the bandwidth requirement for uncompressed video can be immense.

The RFC gives up to 270 Mbps for standard-definition video and approximately 1 Gbps for high-definition video. On best-effort networks, users MUST monitor packet loss and keep loss within the stated TCP-throughput comparison. Senders can use congestion control, or receivers can leave when loss is too high.
sections.plainLanguage: Uncompressed video can consume very high bandwidth. On best-effort networks, users must watch packet loss and respond when the path cannot carry the stream.
